analysis_summary,"Key numeric differences and implications (short analysis):

This quantitative extraction uses the figures summarized in the provided raw_research.md and conservative mapping assumptions where direct pack-level Na‑ion residential data were missing. Central estimates (with uncertainty reflecting reported ranges and manufacturer claim variability) show the following numeric contrasts:

- Energy density: Na‑ion ~137.5 ±37.5 Wh/kg vs Li‑ion (stationary/LFP) ~125 ±35 Wh/kg. Both fit typical stationary needs; Na‑ion central is slightly higher here because many Na‑ion vendors report ~100–175 Wh/kg cell numbers. Normalized scores: Na 35 ±15 vs Li 30 ±14 (scale 50–300 Wh/kg).

- Cost per kWh (cell/pack-level proxy): Na‑ion estimated 90 ±20 USD/kWh vs Li‑ion 100 ±20 USD/kWh. Na‑ion scores higher on price (68.8 vs 62.5 normalized) reflecting manufacturer claims of lower raw‑material cost; independent audited pack‑level data for residential Na‑ion remain limited.

- Cycle life: Na‑ion central 6,000 ±4,000 cycles (vendors report 2k–10k common; some claim >>50k for niche chemistries) vs LFP central 4,500 ±1,500 cycles. Normalized cycle‑life scores favor Na (~11.1 ±8.1) over Li (~8.1 ±3.0) but absolute normalized values are low because the scoring scale includes very long‑life endpoints (up to 50k cycles).

- Calendar life: Na 12 ±6 years vs Li 10 ±2 years — limited field data for Na means larger uncertainty. Normalized scores: Na 37.9 ±20.7 vs Li 31.0 ±6.9.

- Round‑trip efficiency: Na 88 ±4% vs Li 90 ±3%. Normalized: Na 72 ±16 vs Li 80 ±12. Li‑ion has a modest edge in energy throughput efficiency at pack/system level based on available datasheets.

- Usable DoD: Na assumed 80 ±10% vs Li (LFP) 90 ±5% — Li has higher usable fraction in typical residential product designs.

- Operating temperature width: modeled widths (Na 90 ±10 C vs Li 75 ±8 C) produce higher normalized score for Na (83.3 vs 58.3) reflecting vendor statements of robust high/low‑temp behavior for Na chemistry, but real system tolerance depends on pack BMS and enclosure.

- Safety & recycling: Li‑ion (LFP) scores higher for safety (85 ±5) and recycling maturity (80 ±10) compared with Na‑ion (75 ±10 safety; 50 ±15 recycling) because Li‑ion residential systems have broader UL/system certification and an established recycling industry.

Weighted overall suitability (weights explained above) yields central scores: Na‑ion 55.8 ±13.7 (range ~42–69.5) and Li‑ion (LFP) 58.2 ±8.7 (range ~49.5–66.9). The two technologies are close in overall suitability for residential use under current evidence: Li‑ion (LFP) maintains a small lead driven by higher safety/recycling maturity and slightly better RTE and usable DoD, while Na‑ion competes on cost, operating temperature robustness, and potentially longer cycle life in some vendor claims.

Interpretation and next steps:
- For most homeowners today, LFP‑based Li‑ion systems remain the lower‑risk choice because of better documented pack‑level performance, UL/system listings, warranties, and recycling channels. The computed scores reflect that institutional maturity.
- Na‑ion is promising and may surpass Li‑ion on cost and longevity when residential‑grade packs, standardized warranties, and system certifications are widely available; uncertainty is the dominant factor in Na‑ion estimates and should be reduced by independent pack‑level datasheets and field trials.
- Suggested follow‑ups: obtain vendor pack datasheets (residential Na‑ion pilot products), independent RTE/efficiency measurements, and audited cost‑per‑pack studies to reduce uncertainties and refine the suitability comparison.

Note: all numeric mappings and normalization scales are documented above and reflect conservative choices to favor residential priorities (safety, cost, longevity). This CSV embeds both the raw central estimates with uncertainty and the normalized/weighted outputs used to reach the summary conclusion."
